summary: Makes the AES Key Wrap algorithm conveniently available to the Internet community. Its text is largely taken from a NIST draft. The algorithm is meant for encrypting other cryptographic keys with an AES key.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 3394 defines a way to encrypt cryptographic key data with an AES key. When the data is unwrapped, a built-in check detects corruption; the method does not protect the AES key used to wrap it.

subtitle: How to wrap key data with AES and check its integrity when it is unwrapped.

tldr.problem: Cryptographic keys and other data need a defined way to be encrypted with an AES key while also checking for corruption.
tldr.mechanism: AES Key Wrap processes the data in 64-bit blocks, adds a 64-bit integrity value, and performs six AES steps per data block. Unwrapping reverses the steps and checks the value.
tldr.outcome: A failed integrity check requires an error and no returned key data. The key-encryption key must also be protected from disclosure.

today: RFC 3394 is an Informational RFC, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It specifies the AES Key Wrap algorithm and its default initial value.

sections.title: Purpose and Key Terms
sections.content:
RFC 3394 makes the Advanced Encryption Standard (AES) Key Wrap algorithm available to the Internet community. The algorithm encrypts key data together with integrity information, and the wrapped result can be longer than one AES block.

The RFC uses key data for whatever data is being wrapped, whether or not it is actually a key. The key used to wrap that data is the key-encryption key (KEK). The KEK is a valid AES key of 128, 192, or 256 bits.
sections.plainLanguage: The algorithm encrypts key data with a separate AES key called the key-encryption key. The data can include keys or other values.

sections.title: Blocks and Inputs
sections.content:
Before wrapping, the input is divided into n blocks of 64 bits. The algorithm requires at least two blocks and sets no upper limit on their number. Data of 64 bits or less does not need this wrapping process under the specification.

The algorithm works with each supported AES key size. The KEK size affects overall security, but not the wrapping steps. The process uses 6n steps and produces n+1 blocks of 64 bits, so the result includes one extra block.
sections.plainLanguage: The input is split into 64-bit pieces. The algorithm requires at least two pieces and adds one more piece to the wrapped result.

sections.title: Wrapping and Unwrapping
sections.content:
Wrapping starts with a 64-bit register set to the initial value and the input blocks in an array of registers. Each of the 6n steps encrypts the register and first data block with AES. The step number is mixed into the upper half of the result, while the lower half becomes a data block. The final register and all data blocks form the wrapped output.

Unwrapping starts from the wrapped blocks and runs the calculations in reverse with AES decryption. The RFC gives both a shifting description and an index-based description that can operate in place. If the recovered initial value is acceptable, the algorithm returns the data blocks; otherwise it returns an error.
sections.plainLanguage: Wrapping repeatedly encrypts the integrity register together with a data block and mixes in the step number. Unwrapping reverses those steps and returns the data only if the final check succeeds.

sections.title: The Initial Value Checks Integrity
sections.content:
The initial value is placed in the 64-bit register before wrapping. During unwrapping, the recovered value is compared with the expected initial value. A match accepts the key data; a mismatch requires an error.

The default initial value is A6A6A6A6A6A6A6A6. If unwrapping recovers this value, the RFC gives the chance that the key data is corrupt as 2^-64. If it recovers any other value, the implementation MUST return an error and MUST NOT return key data. The RFC also allows alternative initial values for applications that need a different integrity scope.
sections.plainLanguage: When the data is unwrapped, the algorithm checks whether the original 64-bit value has returned. If it has not, the implementation must return an error and no key data.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The integrity check helps detect corruption while the key data is wrapped. A mismatch must produce an error without returning any of the data. The RFC states that the chance of corrupt data producing the default check value is 2^-64.

The KEK needs separate protection. If someone obtains the KEK, they may be able to disclose all key data wrapped with it. The algorithm does not remove that key-management responsibility.
sections.plainLanguage: The integrity check can detect corruption, but it does not protect the KEK itself. Anyone who obtains that key may expose the data it protects.
